rules.title: Shared Mutable Instance State Without Isolation
rules.problemContext: Mutable instance state can race when it is exposed through shared access or reached from multiple concurrency contexts.
rules.expectedBehavior: Shared mutable instance state should have one visible isolation or synchronization boundary.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when mutable instance state is reachable through a visible global or static shared instance, or is visibly accessed from multiple concurrency contexts, and no actor isolation or synchronization protects it. Report the state and its visible access path. Mutation of the global or static stored value itself belongs to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-004.

rules.title: Replaceable Task Without Lifecycle Management
rules.problemContext: Repeated unstructured work can let an older task overwrite newer results.
rules.expectedBehavior: Replaceable work should cancel, supersede, or reject stale tasks.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs only when the analysed file shows replaceable unstructured tasks, a visible path that starts newer work before older work completes, updates from both tasks to the same result target, and no cancellation or stale-result guard. Do not infer repeated invocation from callers outside the file. Independent detached work belongs to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-007.

rules.title: Unjustified Unsafe Concurrency Escape Hatch
rules.problemContext: Unsafe concurrency annotations move safety responsibility from the compiler to the developer.
rules.expectedBehavior: An unsafe opt-out should have a visible safety mechanism or invariant.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs only when the analysed file uses @unchecked Sendable, nonisolated(unsafe), @preconcurrency, or assumeIsolated and also shows mutable state or access that relies on that opt-out without a visible safety invariant or protection mechanism. The annotation alone is insufficient. Do not infer missing protection from code outside the file. An ordinary non-Sendable transfer belongs to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-006.

rules.title: Unprotected Mutable Global or Static State
rules.problemContext: Mutable global or static state can be reached from unrelated concurrency contexts.
rules.expectedBehavior: Mutable global or static state should be immutable, actor-isolated, or synchronized.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when mutable global or static stored state itself is visibly read or written from multiple concurrency contexts without isolation or synchronization. A shared reference to mutable instance state belongs to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-001; do not flag the reference here unless the stored reference itself is reassigned concurrently.

rules.title: Unsafe Actor State Assumption After Suspension
rules.problemContext: Actor-isolated state can change while an actor method is suspended.
rules.expectedBehavior: Code should not assume actor state remains unchanged across await without validating or snapshotting it.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when an actor method establishes or reads mutable state, suspends, and then relies on that state still having its earlier value without validation. Actor access without this stale-state assumption is not a violation.

rules.title: Non-Sendable Value Crossing an Isolation Boundary
rules.problemContext: A non-Sendable value can become unsafe when transferred and then used from another isolation region.
rules.expectedBehavior: Transferred values should be Sendable, remain in one isolation region, or use a valid ownership transfer such as sending.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs only when the analysed file visibly establishes that a value is non-Sendable, transfers that value across an actor or task boundary, and retains conflicting access after the transfer. If Sendable conformance or ownership depends on a declaration outside the file, omit the finding. Explicit unsafe annotations belong to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-003.

rules.title: Inappropriate Detached Task
rules.problemContext: A detached task does not inherit priority, task-local values, or cancellation state.
rules.expectedBehavior: Task.detached should be limited to work intentionally independent of its initiating task and actor context.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when Task.detached performs work that visibly depends on the parent task's cancellation, task-local values, priority, or actor-owned state. Replaceable stale work belongs to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-002.

rules.title: Long-Running Task Ignores Cancellation
rules.problemContext: Cancellation is cooperative, so long-running work continues until it observes cancellation.
rules.expectedBehavior: Loops and repeated asynchronous work should check or propagate cancellation at suitable points.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a visible long-running loop or repeated operation can continue after cancellation because it neither checks cancellation nor exits through a cancellation-throwing operation. Task replacement belongs to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-002.

rules.title: Unobserved Throwing Task-Group Failure
rules.problemContext: Throwing task-group child errors are observed through group result retrieval.
rules.expectedBehavior: A throwing task group should consume child results with for try await, next(), reduce(), or an equivalent throwing operation.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when withThrowingTaskGroup adds throwing child tasks but the group body never performs a throwing result-consumption operation.

rules.title: Blocking Operation in Async Context
rules.problemContext: Blocking a cooperative-pool thread can delay unrelated asynchronous work.
rules.expectedBehavior: Asynchronous code should suspend rather than block while waiting.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when an async function or Task waits with Thread.sleep, a semaphore, a blocking lock wait, or an equivalent synchronous blocking operation. Short synchronous computation is not a violation.

rules.title: Task Ownership Retain Cycle
rules.problemContext: An owner that stores a Task can form a retain cycle when the Task strongly captures that owner.
rules.expectedBehavior: A stored long-running Task should avoid strongly retaining its owner or guarantee termination independently.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when an object stores a long-running or repeating Task and that Task strongly captures the same object, allowing the Task to prevent owner deallocation. One-way retention by a short-lived unstored Task is not a violation.

rules.title: Incomplete AsyncStream Lifecycle
rules.problemContext: A stream that never finishes or releases producer resources can remain active indefinitely.
rules.expectedBehavior: A finite AsyncStream should finish on every terminal path, and bridged resources should be released through termination handling.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs only when the analysed file establishes that an AsyncStream is finite and shows a terminal path without finish, or when the file creates a bridged observer, delegate, or producer whose cleanup responsibility is visible but supplies no matching onTermination cleanup. Do not infer finiteness, termination, or cleanup responsibility from external code.

rules.title: Multiple Consumers of a Single AsyncStream
rules.problemContext: A single AsyncStream distributes elements instead of broadcasting every element to every consumer.
rules.expectedBehavior: Code that requires broadcast delivery should create separate streams or use a broadcast-capable design.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs only when the analysed file shows the same AsyncStream instance being iterated by multiple tasks and visibly establishes that every consumer must receive every element. Multiple consumers alone are insufficient; do not infer broadcast intent from external callers or naming alone.

rules.title: Unjustified Force Unwrapping
rules.problemContext: Swift optionals represent values that may be absent. Force unwrapping bypasses the language's optional-safety mechanisms and causes a runtime failure when the optional contains nil.
rules.expectedBehavior: Optional values should normally be handled using optional binding, guard statements, optional chaining, nil coalescing, or another safe mechanism. Force unwrapping should only be used when the non-nil invariant is clearly guaranteed by the visible code or surrounding API contract.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when an optional value is force-unwrapped and the visible code does not establish a reliable guarantee that the value cannot be nil at the point of access.

rules.title: Unnecessary Implicitly Unwrapped Optional
rules.problemContext: Implicitly unwrapped optionals allow values to be accessed without explicit optional handling and can introduce runtime crashes when initialization assumptions are violated. They may also hide incomplete dependency initialization.
rules.expectedBehavior: Properties should normally be initialized as non-optional values when they are required dependencies or represented as regular optionals when absence is valid. Implicitly unwrapped optionals should be limited to situations where delayed initialization is required and reliably guaranteed.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a property is declared as an implicitly unwrapped optional without a visible requirement for delayed guaranteed initialization, particularly when the property represents a dependency that could instead be supplied during initialization.

rules.title: Unjustified Force Try
rules.problemContext: Using try! suppresses Swift's error-handling mechanism and converts a thrown error into a runtime crash. This makes failure conditions unsafe when the operation can legitimately fail.
rules.expectedBehavior: Throwing operations should normally propagate or handle errors using throws, do-catch, Result, or another appropriate error-handling mechanism. Force try should only be used when failure is demonstrably impossible or guaranteed by a controlled invariant.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when try! is used for an operation that can fail and the visible code or surrounding invariant does not provide sufficient evidence that failure is impossible.

rules.title: Strong Reference Cycle in Closure Capture
rules.problemContext: Swift Automatic Reference Counting does not automatically resolve strong reference cycles. A closure stored by an object can capture that same object strongly, preventing both the closure and object from being released.
rules.expectedBehavior: Closures should use capture semantics appropriate to their ownership relationship. When an escaping or stored closure would otherwise create a strong reference cycle, an appropriate weak or unowned capture should be used.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when an object strongly retains a non-Task closure and that closure strongly captures the same object, creating a visible ownership cycle without an appropriate capture strategy to break the cycle. Stored Task ownership cycles belong to ARCA-SWIFT-CONCURRENCY-011.

rules.title: Direct Singleton Service Access
rules.problemContext: Directly accessing a global singleton service from application components creates an implicit dependency that is difficult to substitute, isolate, or control during testing and can introduce shared mutable state.
rules.expectedBehavior: External services and other application dependencies should be supplied explicitly through an appropriate dependency mechanism such as constructor injection, environment-based injection, or an architecture-specific dependency system.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs only when a component directly accesses an operational service through .shared, a global variable, or a service locator instead of receiving that service through an explicit and replaceable dependency boundary. Singleton declarations, shared constants, and a type accessing its own shared actor instance do not constitute violations. Accessing a stored instance property does not, by itself, constitute singleton access.

rules.title: Incorrect SwiftUI State Ownership
rules.problemContext: SwiftUI state wrappers communicate ownership and data-flow semantics. Using @State, @Binding, or observable state for data that is owned elsewhere can create duplicate sources of truth, stale state, or unclear ownership relationships.
rules.expectedBehavior: @State should be used for state owned by the view, @Binding should represent writable state owned by another component, and externally supplied read-only values should normally remain regular properties. Observable state should have a clear owner.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a SwiftUI property wrapper conflicts with the visible ownership of the data, such as using @State for data passed into a view, using @Binding for read-only data, or otherwise creating competing sources of truth.

rules.title: Incompatible Observation Mechanisms
rules.problemContext: SwiftUI provides different observation mechanisms with different lifecycle and ownership semantics. Mixing mechanisms such as the Observation framework and ObservableObject-based wrappers can create redundant observation, misleading ownership semantics, and unnecessary complexity.
rules.expectedBehavior: A type and its consuming views should use an observation mechanism appropriate to the application's platform requirements and should avoid combining incompatible or redundant observation mechanisms without a specific interoperability requirement.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a type using the Observation framework is unnecessarily combined with ObservableObject-related state mechanisms, or when a view applies ownership wrappers that do not correspond to the observation model used by the object.

rules.title: Improper Async Work Lifecycle in SwiftUI View
rules.problemContext: Asynchronous work launched manually from SwiftUI lifecycle callbacks may continue after the view disappears or may require manual cancellation management. SwiftUI provides task modifiers whose lifecycle is associated with the view.
rules.expectedBehavior: View-bound asynchronous work should use SwiftUI task lifecycle mechanisms such as .task or .task(id:) where appropriate so that execution and cancellation correspond to the view lifecycle. Manually created tasks should have an explicit lifecycle reason when used instead.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when view-bound asynchronous work is launched through manual Task creation from lifecycle callbacks such as onAppear or onChange without an apparent need for an independent task lifetime and without equivalent cancellation management.

rules.title: Heavy Computation in SwiftUI View Body
rules.problemContext: SwiftUI may evaluate a view's body repeatedly as state changes. Performing filtering, sorting, mapping, complex calculations, network access, database access, or other expensive work directly during body evaluation can repeat unnecessary work and degrade rendering performance.
rules.expectedBehavior: A SwiftUI view body should primarily describe the view hierarchy. Expensive data transformations, I/O operations, and complex calculations should be performed outside body or moved into an appropriate model, view model, cached computation, or asynchronous operation.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when the body of a SwiftUI view performs substantial data processing, synchronous I/O, networking, database access, or complex computation that may be repeated as part of view rendering.

rules.title: Unnecessary GeometryReader Usage
rules.problemContext: GeometryReader participates in SwiftUI layout and can introduce additional layout complexity. Unnecessary or nested GeometryReader instances can make layouts harder to reason about and may introduce avoidable layout work.
rules.expectedBehavior: GeometryReader should be used when a view genuinely requires information about its available geometry. Simpler layout mechanisms such as flexible frames, container-relative sizing, or appropriate layout APIs should be preferred when they can express the same layout.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when GeometryReader is used without a visible need for geometry information, when it only reproduces behavior available through simpler layout APIs, or when nested GeometryReader instances introduce unnecessary layout complexity.

rules.title: Excessive Observable State Dependency
rules.problemContext: SwiftUI invalidates views when observed state on which they depend changes. Passing broad observable objects through a view hierarchy or observing more state than a view requires can cause unnecessary view updates and increase rendering work.
rules.expectedBehavior: Views should depend only on the state required for their presentation and behavior. Observable state should be scoped so that changes invalidate only the parts of the view hierarchy that actually depend on those changes.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a view observes or receives a broad mutable observable object despite using only a small portion of it, or when the visible state structure causes unrelated state changes to trigger unnecessary updates across a substantial view hierarchy.

rules.title: Business Logic in SwiftUI View
rules.problemContext: SwiftUI views are primarily responsible for describing presentation and handling user interaction. Embedding domain operations, networking, persistence, validation, or substantial business logic directly in a view couples presentation to application behavior and reduces testability and maintainability.
rules.expectedBehavior: SwiftUI views should primarily contain presentation and interaction logic. Business operations, data transformation, validation, networking, persistence, and other application behavior should be delegated to an appropriate model, feature, service, reducer, view model, or other architecture-specific component.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a SwiftUI view directly implements substantial business or domain logic, performs network or persistence operations, or assumes responsibilities that should belong to a separate application or domain component.

rules.title: Legacy Reducer API Usage
rules.problemContext: Modern TCA features define application logic in a reducer body using `Reduce` and reducer composition. The legacy `reduce(into:action:)` API and direct reducer invocation rely on an older pattern and can bypass the normal Store-driven action flow.
rules.expectedBehavior: A TCA feature should define its reducer logic through the reducer body, typically using Reduce and reducer composition operators. Child feature behavior should be composed into the reducer hierarchy or triggered by sending actions through the Store rather than by manually invoking another reducer.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a feature implements its application logic using the legacy reduce(into:action:) reducer API, or when application code directly invokes reduce(into:action:) on another reducer instead of composing that reducer or sending an action through the Store.

rules.title: Legacy TCA View Observation API
rules.problemContext: TCA's modern observation model allows SwiftUI views to observe observable feature state directly through Store. Legacy ViewStore and WithViewStore APIs introduce an older observation layer that is no longer required for features using observable state and can result in unnecessary observation boilerplate.
rules.expectedBehavior: Feature State should use TCA's observable-state mechanism where appropriate, and SwiftUI views should read state and send actions directly through Store. Legacy ViewStore, ViewStoreOf, WithViewStore, and related view-observation wrappers should not be introduced into modern observable features.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a modern TCA feature uses ViewStore, ViewStoreOf, WithViewStore, or equivalent legacy observation APIs where the feature can use ObservableState and direct Store observation instead.

rules.title: Deprecated TaskResult Usage
rules.problemContext: Older TCA code represents the result of asynchronous effects with TaskResult. Modern TCA uses Swift's standard Result type for this purpose, avoiding a framework-specific result wrapper that has been deprecated.
rules.expectedBehavior: Actions representing the outcome of asynchronous work should use Swift Result or another appropriate domain-specific result representation rather than TCA's deprecated TaskResult type.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when TaskResult is used in TCA feature state, actions, effects, or supporting code where Result can represent the asynchronous success or failure.

rules.title: Legacy TCA Binding API
rules.problemContext: Modern TCA derives bindings directly from observable stores. Legacy APIs such as `BindingState`, `BindingViewState`, and `BindingViewStore` belong to the older `ViewStore` model and add unnecessary wrappers to modern features.
rules.expectedBehavior: Bindable feature state should use ObservableState, with the Action domain conforming to BindableAction where necessary and BindingReducer participating in the reducer. SwiftUI views should derive bindings from a bindable Store rather than using legacy BindingState or BindingViewStore mechanisms.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a modern observable TCA feature uses deprecated BindingState, BindingViewState, BindingViewStore, or equivalent legacy binding mechanisms instead of deriving bindings directly from an observable Store.

rules.title: Legacy TCA Presentation API
rules.problemContext: Modern observable TCA features model presentation using `@Presents` state and `PresentationAction`, with SwiftUI presentation driven from scoped store bindings. Store-specific presentation modifiers use the older presentation model.
rules.expectedBehavior: When feature state adopts @ObservableState, optional presentation domains should use @Presents and PresentationAction, be composed using the appropriate presentation reducer operator, and be presented using standard item-driven APIs with a scoped Store binding.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a modern observable TCA feature uses @PresentationState or legacy store-specific presentation modifiers such as sheet(store:) where @Presents and Store-based item presentation are applicable.

rules.title: Bypassing a Controlled TCA Dependency
rules.problemContext: TCA dependencies provide explicit and controllable access to external or nondeterministic behavior such as clocks, dates, UUID generation, networking, persistence, and services. Calling an uncontrolled implementation directly can bypass dependency substitution and make feature behavior harder to test and reproduce.
rules.expectedBehavior: External and nondeterministic operations used by reducer logic should be accessed through the feature's declared TCA dependencies. When a controllable dependency such as uuid, date, clock, or an application client is declared, feature logic should consistently use that dependency rather than constructing or accessing an uncontrolled equivalent.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when reducer logic directly invokes an uncontrolled dependency such as UUID(), Date(), a global service, or another concrete external implementation despite an appropriate TCA dependency being declared or clearly serving that responsibility.

rules.title: Missing Cancellation Management for Cancellable Effect
rules.problemContext: TCA effects may continue beyond the action that starts them. Effects that can be cancelled, replaced by newer work, or stopped by user action need an explicit cancellation mechanism.
rules.expectedBehavior: Asynchronous effects that have a visible cancellation requirement should use an appropriate cancellation identifier and cancellable effect composition, and cancellation actions should cancel the corresponding effect. Independent short-lived effects that do not require cancellation do not need cancellation identifiers.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when the visible feature domain establishes that an effect must be cancellable or replaceable, such as by providing a cancel action or repeatedly starting mutually exclusive work, but the launched effect has no corresponding TCA cancellation mechanism.

rules.title: Unnecessary CombineReducers Wrapper
rules.problemContext: CombineReducers is useful when a group of reducers must be combined before applying reducer modifiers such as ifLet or forEach. Wrapping reducers in CombineReducers when no modifier needs to operate on the combined reducer adds an unnecessary composition layer and obscures the reducer hierarchy.
rules.expectedBehavior: Reducers should normally be composed directly in the reducer body. CombineReducers should be introduced when multiple reducers need to be grouped as a unit before a reducer modifier is applied.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when CombineReducers wraps one or more reducers but the resulting group is not used as the base for a modifier or another composition requirement that needs the reducers to be grouped together.

rules.title: Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted in Private Storage
rules.problemContext: Mobile applications may persist sensitive information such as credentials, authentication tokens, cryptographic material, or personal data in private application storage without sufficient protection. If the application sandbox or device is compromised, this information may become accessible.
rules.expectedBehavior: Sensitive information stored locally should be protected using storage mechanisms appropriate to the type of data, such as the iOS Keychain for credentials and cryptographic material or suitable data-protection and encryption mechanisms for application files.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when sensitive information is persisted in private application storage without appropriate protection, for example by storing credentials, tokens, passwords, cryptographic material, or sensitive personal data in plaintext using mechanisms such as UserDefaults, unencrypted files, or insufficiently protected local databases.

rules.title: Insertion of Sensitive Data into Logs
rules.problemContext: Application logs used for debugging and diagnostics can expose sensitive data when credentials, authentication tokens, personal information, cryptographic material, or other secrets are included in log messages.
rules.expectedBehavior: Sensitive user or application data should not be written to logs. Diagnostic messages should contain only the information required for debugging, with sensitive values omitted or appropriately redacted.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when sensitive data is passed to system logging APIs, console output, custom loggers, or third-party logging services without appropriate redaction.

rules.title: God Object Candidate
rules.problemContext: A God Object occurs when a Swift type accumulates substantial knowledge or behavior across several unrelated concerns. This centralization produces weak cohesion, broad dependencies, and a type that becomes difficult to understand, test, change, and maintain.
rules.expectedBehavior: A Swift type should have a focused and cohesive responsibility. Its properties and methods should contribute to that responsibility, while unrelated domain, persistence, networking, presentation, navigation, or coordination concerns should remain under appropriate ownership.
rules.violationCriteria: A violation occurs when a Swift type owns substantial state or behavior for multiple unrelated concerns, demonstrated by distinct groups of properties and methods serving different responsibilities.
